clue.text: Play this or nothing?

definitions.meaning: a comedy by Harold Brighouse, set in a Salford boot shop
the phrase for an offer with no real alternative: take what is given or go without

explanation.surface: A theatregoer is offered one show or none at all.
explanation.walkthrough: Thomas Hobson, a Cambridge stable owner, made customers take the horse nearest the door or none, hence the phrase; Brighouse's 1915 play borrows it.
explanation.definitionFit: The title names a well-known English stage comedy, and the idiom describes a take-it-or-leave-it choice.

clue.text: Period piece in igloo starts off melting

indicators.note: melting suggests the letters flowing into a new shape, so they are rearranged
the starts of the three words are taken off, leaving each word without its opening letter

explanation.surface: Part of an igloo is melting away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'starts off' removes P, I and I from 'piece in igloo', leaving IECE N GLOO, and 'melting' rearranges those nine letters.
explanation.definitionFit: The Oligocene is a geological epoch, a span of time roughly 34 to 23 million years ago.

clue.text: Sickly children coming up to the Fourth of July

indicators.note: in a down entry the first piece sits on top of, and so comes up to, the next one

parts.note: seed is an old word for offspring or descendants

indicators.note: the fourth letter of the word July is taken

explanation.surface: Children fall ill just before Independence Day.
explanation.walkthrough: 'coming up to' looks like a reversal sign, but here SEED simply sits above Y in the down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: Seedy can mean slightly unwell or under the weather, a synonym of sickly.

clue.text: North America's partner, in a manner of speaking

parts.note: NA is an abbreviation for North America, with the possessive S kept
an ally is a partner in a cause

explanation.surface: A country's partner is, so to speak, a friend of North America.
explanation.definitionFit: Speaking nasally is a manner of speaking through the nose, so the adverb describes how one talks.

clue.text: Best name given to the Big Apple's mud pie

parts.note: Calum Best, son of footballer George Best, gives a first name
the Big Apple is New York, abbreviated NY

explanation.surface: A footballer's son has a dessert named after him in New York.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Best' looks like 'finest' but is the surname of George Best; Chambers lists mud pie as a term for an insult.
explanation.definitionFit: Calumny is slander, and mud slung at someone, a mud pie, is a figurative insult.

clue.text: Debauched stoic with unlimited Viagra supply

indicators.note: supply read as supple-ly, in a pliable way, tells us to bend the letters into a new order
the outer letters of the word Viagra are removed, leaving its interior

explanation.surface: A stoic is corrupted by access to unlimited little blue pills.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unlimited' strips the V and A from Viagra to leave IAGR, and 'supply' rearranges STOIC with those letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Orgiastic behaviour is wild and dissolute, much like debauched conduct.

clue.text: Exhibition of Toulouse-Lautrec (or other artist)

indicators.note: an exhibition shows something, here letters on view within the words

explanation.surface: A gallery shows Toulouse-Lautrec or another painter.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters run across the end of Lautrec and the words 'or other'.
explanation.definitionFit: Jean-Baptiste-Camille Corot was a French landscape painter of the nineteenth century.

clue.text: Play the standard way

parts.note: a standard is a level of quality
a street is a way or road

explanation.surface: Acting in the conventional manner.
explanation.walkthrough: Quality Street is a J. M. Barrie comedy; British readers know the name better as a tin of chocolates.
explanation.definitionFit: The title names a Barrie stage comedy first performed in 1901.

clue.text: Play Vladimir or Estragon in mime?

definitions.meaning: a one-act Harold Pinter piece about two hitmen in a basement
the two tramps of Beckett's Waiting for Godot wait all play long, so either, made silent in mime, is a mute waiter

explanation.surface: An actor plays Beckett's characters without speaking.
explanation.walkthrough: A dumbwaiter is also a small service lift, the device at the heart of Pinter's plot.
explanation.definitionFit: The title names a Pinter one-act play, and a waiter who is mute fits the second reading.

clue.text: Doctor v Nurse: a film's content for all to see

indicators.note: to doctor something is to tamper with it, so these letters are rearranged
the content of a word is what lies inside, so the outer letters of film are dropped

explanation.surface: A medical drama pits a doctor against a nurse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'content' takes the inside of film, and 'Doctor' rearranges those letters with V, Nurse and A; U is the British film certificate for all ages.
explanation.definitionFit: In the British film rating system a U certificate marks a picture suitable for every audience.

clue.text: Measure from right, right around

indicators.note: around turns the run of letters back to front
from here signals taking a run of letters out of the words that follow

explanation.surface: Measure all the way round, starting from the right.
explanation.walkthrough: The run HTRIG straddles the two words 'right, right', and 'around' turns it backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Girth is a measurement around the middle of something, such as a waist or tree trunk.

clue.text: Potty adult's potty? Extremely potty!

parts.note: a grown-up's equivalent of a child's potty is the toilet, informally the loo

indicators.note: the extreme, outermost letters of the word potty are taken

explanation.surface: A child's potty, an adult's potty, utterly potty!
explanation.walkthrough: Potty appears three times in three senses: crazy, the toilet, and as plain fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Loopy and potty are both British informal words for mildly crazy.

clue.text: Beat meat, like '50s male

parts.note: lamb is a meat
as means like, in the same way
a Ted, short for Teddy boy, was a 1950s British youth in Edwardian-style dress

explanation.surface: Meat that beats, like a 1950s man.
explanation.definitionFit: To lambast is to thrash or beat severely, so the past form matches beat.

clue.text: Solomon's head due to be splashed in some water then?

definitions.text: Solomon's head due to be splashed in some water then?

indicators.note: one piece sits inside the river's name

parts.note: the Tay is a Scottish river

indicators.note: splashed water scatters, so the letters are thrown into a new order
the head of a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: Solomon Grundy's christening, with his head about to be wetted.
explanation.walkthrough: The nursery rhyme runs 'Solomon Grundy, born on a Monday, christened on Tuesday': the whole clue describes his baptism day. 'to be splashed' rearranges S and DUE into UESD.
explanation.definitionFit: In the rhyme the christening, with water on the head, falls on this day of the week.

clue.text: Crazy recipe replaced by chef's starter, so mouth-watering

indicators.note: one letter gives way to another in the word

parts.note: delirious means wildly excited or crazy
R, from Latin recipe, is the abbreviation heading a prescription

indicators.note: a starter comes first, so the first letter of the word chef's is used

explanation.surface: A chef's starter makes a crazy recipe so tasty.
explanation.definitionFit: Something mouth-watering looks or smells tasty, which is exactly what delicious food is.

clue.text: Rare element of mildly obscene, topless turns touring Indonesia

indicators.note: touring means going round, so one piece surrounds the other
turns reverses the order of the remaining letters
topless removes the top, the first letter

parts.note: smutty means slightly rude or indecent
RI is the international vehicle code for Indonesia

explanation.surface: A risqué topless show goes on tour in Indonesia.
explanation.walkthrough: 'topless' drops the first letter, 'turns' reads what is left backwards as YTTUM, and 'touring' sends it round the vehicle code.
explanation.definitionFit: Yttrium is a rare-earth metallic element, atomic number 39.

clue.text: In running for cover, lesbian freely admits "game up"

indicators.note: admits means lets in, so one piece goes inside the other
freely suggests the letters move without constraint into a new order
in a down entry, up means the letters read from bottom to top

parts.note: RU is rugby union, a game

explanation.surface: A lesbian openly confesses the game is up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'freely' rearranges LESBIAN into INSABLE, which takes in UR, RU turned by 'up'.
explanation.definitionFit: Being insurable means being eligible, in the running, for an insurance policy.

clue.text: Female to demand backing material for record

parts.note: she refers to a female

indicators.note: backing means going backwards, so the letters are reversed

parts.note: a call is a demand, as in a call for action

explanation.surface: A woman insists on support for her recording.
explanation.definitionFit: Shellac resin was the material from which 78 rpm gramophone records were pressed.

clue.text: Lame duck's third to make waves

indicators.note: the third letter of the word duck's is taken

parts.note: to ripple is to form small waves

explanation.surface: A lame duck causes a stir.
explanation.definitionFit: To lame is to disable a limb, the same as to cripple, both verbs.

clue.text: County dread losing English opener, a great cutter

parts.note: Bucks is short for Buckinghamshire, an English county

indicators.note: losing means a letter is taken away

parts.note: awe is dread mixed with wonder

indicators.note: the opener of a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: A county fears losing England's opening batsman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'English opener' sounds like cricket, but it is just the E that starts English.
explanation.definitionFit: A bucksaw is a large two-handed saw set in a frame, a big cutting tool.

clue.text: Research scientist (apparently) out, entertaining fit guy: not hard to play hooky

indicators.note: to entertain is to host, so one piece holds the other
out says the word in is removed

parts.note: boffin is British slang for a research scientist

indicators.note: H is the pencil abbreviation for hard, and it is dropped

parts.note: a hunk is an attractive, well-built man

explanation.surface: A scientist leaves, taking a handsome man with him, to skip work.
explanation.walkthrough: '(apparently)' hints that BOFFIN reads as BOFF + IN; 'out' leaves BOFF. 'not hard' leaves UNK from HUNK. Bunk off is British slang for skipping school.
explanation.definitionFit: To bunk off is to truant or skip school, the British equivalent of playing hooky.

clue.text: Muscles working to absorb iron in meal

indicators.note: to absorb is to take in, so one piece goes inside another

parts.note: recti is the plural of rectus, a straight muscle such as in the abdomen
Fe is the chemical symbol for iron
on means working or operating

explanation.surface: Exercised muscles take in iron from food.
explanation.definitionFit: Refection is an old word for a light meal or refreshment.

clue.text: Binge eating primarily found in tipsy lovelorn …

indicators.note: found in says one letter sits inside another piece
tipsy suggests the letters stagger into a new order
lovelorn means losing love, the O of a zero score

parts.note: the ellipsis runs on to the next clue, whose answer is the fodder here

indicators.note: primarily picks the first letter of the word eating

explanation.surface: A drunk, heartbroken overweight man goes on an eating binge.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis links to 23 down: its answer loses O for 'lovelorn' and 'tipsy' rearranges the rest to FAST, round E.
explanation.definitionFit: A feast is a large meal, a bout of overindulgence much like a binge.

clue.text: What whistle-blower may say about a physicist

indicators.note: about means turned around, so the letters are read backwards

parts.note: a referee blows the whistle and might announce 'I'm ref'

explanation.surface: A whistle-blower talks about a scientist.
explanation.walkthrough: A whistle-blower usually means an informer, but here it is a referee.
explanation.definitionFit: Enrico Fermi was an Italian-born physicist who built the first nuclear reactor.

clue.text: … person that's overweight, finally breaking settee after part exchange

annotationWithheld.why: … person that's overweight, finally breaking settee after part exchange: T, the last letter of 'overweight', breaks SOFA with SO and FA swapped, but 'overweight' is also needed in the definition, so one word does two jobs
annotationWithheld.clue: … person that's overweight, finally breaking settee after part exchange

clue.text: Revered female poets regularly are reflecting

indicators.note: reflecting means mirrored, so the joined letters read backwards
regularly takes every other letter of the word poets

explanation.surface: Women poets are regularly thoughtful.
explanation.walkthrough: 'regularly' gives OT from POETS; OTARE read back by 'reflecting' gives the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Erato is the Muse of lyric and love poetry, a goddess honoured by poets.

clue.text: Pot ball flukily here at last, having previously pocketed nothing?

definitions.text: Pot ball flukily here at last, having previously pocketed nothing?

indicators.note: pocketed means taken inside, so one piece goes into the other
a fluke is a lucky shot, so the letters land in a chance order
at last takes the final letter of the word here

parts.note: O is nothing, a zero

explanation.surface: A snooker player finally pots a ball by luck after a barren spell.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue describes the place where it happens: a lucky pot after a run of misses.
explanation.definitionFit: A pool table is where one pots balls into pockets, the setting of the scene described.

clue.text: Play sonata with feet only, your hands initially being incapacitated

indicators.note: incapacitated suggests the letters are disabled and jumbled
initially takes the first letter of each of the three words

explanation.surface: A pianist plays a sonata with feet alone, hands out of action.
explanation.walkthrough: 'initially' gives O, Y and H; 'being incapacitated' rearranges them with the two printed words before them. Shelagh Delaney wrote the play at nineteen.
explanation.definitionFit: This is Shelagh Delaney's 1958 stage play set in Salford.
